title: Contextual Caching & Prefix Strategies — conference scrapbook
content:
Quick context: attended an afternoon of talks focused on long-context strategies and caching at the mini-symposium (unofficial notes). Goal: capture interesting ideas we might try for Redwood Optimize and the serving runtime experiments. Lots of rough fragments — intended as a personal scratchpad and to seed a small spike.

Top takeaways (short):
- Paper A (Sparse Prefix Trees for Cacheable Prompts) — idea: index prefix fragments by rolling-hash of tokenized prompt windows, enable partial KV reuse even when prompt slightly shifts. Could be cheaper than full LRU because index size smaller. Think about collision rate and multi-length buckets.
- Blog post B (Practical Layerwise KV Compression) — lossy compress older KV entries with coachmarks: keep attention-critical heads dense, compress rest to 4-bit and sparse rows. Promising for sessions where early tokens are rarely re-attended.
- Talk C (Adaptive Cache Eviction via UX Signal) — use application-level metrics (latency budget, token budget, error on hallucination checks) to inform TTL. TTLs become dynamic per-customer route.

Notes / questions to explore:
- How to measure "reuse value" of a prefix? Candidate metric: delta in perplexity or next-token predictive entropy when we drop prefix entries from KV. Cheap proxy: log-prob change on a small validation prompt set. But that's latency-expensive.
- Implementation idea: maintain shadow-sampled deltas for 0.1% of requests: on those, compute with and without cached prefix and log delta to estimate utility distribution. Use that to inform global eviction policy.
- Combine rolling-hash prefix index with similarity-based candidate matching (embedding of last N tokens) so we can reuse cache entries even when exact tokens differ due to template variables.

Mini experiment plan (3 days):
1) Proxy-level rolling-hash index PoC: integrate a small in-memory map keyed by 64-bit rolling hash computed over token ids for last 64 tokens. Attach pointer to KV snapshot ID and timestamp. On request, probe with 64/128/256 windows and measure average KV reuse and lookup cost.
   - Success metric: >5% token compute saved for internal conversational traces at 95th percentile latency unchanged.
2) Shadow delta sampler: pick 0.5% of requests, run them with and without cache (or with truncated cache) and compute token loss delta. Aggregate per-route and per-customer.
   - Use this to drive TTL suggestions in Optimize UI.
3) Tiny layerwise compression bench: evaluate applying 4-bit compression to non-top-2 heads on GPT-like model; measure top-1 token degradation on held-out prompts.

Experimental details / commands (scratch):
- rolling-hash snippet (pseudo):
  hash = 1469598103934665603
  for t in tokens[-window:]:
    hash = (hash ^ t) * 1099511628211 & ((1<<64)-1)
  // store hash -> {kv_snapshot_id, seq_len, created_at}

- sampling flags in runtime: enable --cache-shadow-sample-rate=0.005
- data to collect: route, model, cache_hit(bool), hash_key, kv_snapshot_age, delta_logprob(token-level avg)

Practical caveats raised in talks:
- Hash collisions create silent wrong reuse; need cheap verification step (replay first M tokens of matched cache at lower precision) before applying full KV.
- Memory amplification when storing many partial snapshots; consider storing diffs from checkpoint instead of full copies.
- Privacy: storing prefixes could unintentionally capture PII. We must integrate KMS tagging and optional per-customer opt-out in Private mode. For Hosted API, need clear docs and opt-out flags.

Ideas to make this unique for Redwood Optimize / Runtime:
- Expose per-route cache utility curve: x-axis TTL, y-axis token-savings. Show suggested TTLs with expected cost delta and 95th latency impact.
- Provide a "cache rehearsal" job in Dedicated that warms cache across replicas at rollout time (can dramatically reduce cold-start p99s for chatty tenants).
- A/B for cache: compare canonical vs adaptive TTL; route fallback to non-cached model variant if mismatch detected.

Related reading (links I scribbled down):
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.00001 (Sparse Prefix Trees — placeholder id; need to download)
- https://blog.example.com/layerwise-kv-compression
- https://acmeconf.org/2026/session/long-context-caching

Meeting/Follow-ups:
- Sync with Owen to see if the rolling-hash PoC can piggyback on his request-trace extractor (INF-2147).
- Ask Maya for sample traces that include template-variable prompts (customer support transcripts) — those are where similarity-match reuse might shine.
- Draft a short note for Optimize: "Cache TTL suggestions: how we measure benefit" (one-pager for PM review).

Loose thoughts (brain dump):
- Could we do probabilistic prefix matching with Bloom filters at the proxy to avoid heavy embedding cost? Use two-stage: bloom -> verify.
- Think about pricing model: highlight token-savings from cache as a positive ROI to upsell Dedicated.
- If we can detect session semantics (instruction vs. content-heavy), adapt cache aggressiveness: e.g., do not cache personal-data heavy content.

TODO (short):
- [ ] Write the PoC proxy module skeleton (2d)
- [ ] Add shadow sampler flag and telemetry to runtime (1d)
- [ ] Pull privacy/legal on storing prefixes (ASAP)
- [ ] Create a tiny dashboard in Console showing cache-hit percent by route (spike)

Endnotes: this is messy — keep it intentionally lightweight. Revisit after PoC runs and fill in measured numbers. If results good, promote to a product PRD and link to Optimize UX mockups.

-- Arun
